page.title: Tramadol (strong painkiller)
about: Find out how tramadol treats moderate to severe pain and how to take it.
• Tramadol is not suitable for everyone. For example, check with your doctor if you have breathing difficulty or kidney problems.
• Tramadol comes as tablets, capsules and liquid that you swallow. Follow your doctor’s instructions about how to take it because it can be addictive.
• Common side effects of tramadol include feeling sick and dizzy. More serious side effects can happen in rare cases.
• It can cause problems to take tramadol with some other medicines, such as medicines for depression, anxiety or allergy symptoms.

lines.text: Most adults and children aged 12 years old and over can take tramadol.

cards.headline: Who may not be able to take tramadol

lines.text: Tramadol is not suitable for some people. To make sure it's safe for you, before starting the medicine, tell your doctor or pharmacist if you:
have ever had an allergic reaction to tramadol or any other medicine
have a condition which causes seizures or fits
have a head injury
have an addiction to alcohol, strong painkillers or recreational drugs
have breathing difficulties
have kidney or liver problems
ever had a reaction to other strong painkillers
are pregnant, breastfeeding, or trying to get pregnant
How to take standard tablets and capsules
Swallow each tramadol tablet or capsule whole with a glass of water.
Mix the drops into a glass of water then drink the whole contents of the glass.
Dissolve each tablet in 50ml of water and drink the whole contents of the glass.

Make sure your hands are dry before handling the tablet. Pop the tablet out of its pack and put it on your tongue. Suck the tablet, do not chew it. After it has melted, swallow or have a drink of water.
You can also dissolve the tablet in a small glass of water if you prefer.
It's important to swallow slow-release tramadol tablets and capsules whole with a drink of water.
Slow-release tablets and capsules release the medicine into your body over either 12 or 24 hours. This type of tramadol takes longer to start working but lasts longer. It's used for severe pain.
Important

Do not break, crush, chew or suck slow-release tablets and capsules. If you do, the slow-release system will not happen and the whole dose might get into your body immediately. This could cause an overdose, which can be dangerous.
When to take tramadol
When to take it depends on the type of tramadol you have been prescribed:
standard tablets and capsules – usually 3 to 4 times a day
drops – usually 3 to 4 times a day
slow-release tablets and capsules – usually once or twice a day
If you're 65 or over, or you have liver or kidney problems, your doctor may tell you to take tramadol less often.

You can take tramadol at any time of day but try to take it at the same time every day, and space your doses evenly. For example, if you take tramadol twice a day and have your first dose at 8am, take your second dose at 8pm.
These common side effects of tramadol happen to more than 1 in 100 people. There are things you can do to help cope with them.
Headaches
Feeling sleepy, tired, dizzy or "spaced out"
Feeling or being sick (nausea or vomiting)
Constipation
Dry mouth
Sweating
Low energy
It is important to treat pain in pregnancy.
If you have severe pain, tramadol might be your best option. Your doctor can help you decide what's right for you and your baby. It’s always best to only take tramadol for a few days if possible.
Tramadol is not known to cause problems with your baby’s development, but more studies are required to confirm this.

If you take tramadol at the end of pregnancy your baby might have withdrawal symptoms when they’re born, such as feeding problems or needing help with breathing. If this happens, your baby may be monitored in hospital for a few days after birth.
If you are taking tramadol regularly then discuss this with your doctor or midwife.

If your baby is healthy, you may be able to take tramadol while breastfeeding. However, it’s best to only take tramadol for a few days if possible. If you need to take it for longer, talk to your doctor who may recommend a different painkiller.
Tramadol passes into breast milk in very small amounts, and it’s unlikely to cause any side effects in your baby. However, it might cause your baby to be sleepy.
It's very rare for breastfed babies to have side effects from medicines you're taking. But it's important to keep monitoring your baby if you're taking any medicine while breastfeeding.
Contact your healthcare professional or call 111 as soon as possible if you notice that your baby:
is not feeding as well as usual, or gaining weight as you’d expect
seems unusually sleepy
seems unusually irritable
is constipated or being sick
It’s important to not share a bed with your baby while you’re taking tramadol.
Information
Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
Bring all the medicines you or your baby takes with you.
your baby has breathing problems
Ask for advice about whether to keep breastfeeding and taking your medicine.
Some medicines can affect the way tramadol works and increase the chances of you having side effects.
Before taking tramadol, tell your doctor if you're already taking any other medicines, including any medicines that:
treat depression or other mental health problems
relieve pain
help you sleep
reduce tension or anxiety
treat symptoms of an allergy
help prevent blood clots (such as warfarin)
treat an infection
Some medicines may weaken or shorten the effect of tramadol. Tell your doctor if you're taking:
carbamazepine to treat epilepsy
buprenorphine, a painkiller
ondansetron, to stop you feeling sick
rifampicin, an antibiotic
These are not all the medicines that may cause problems if you take them with tramadol. For a full list, see the leaflet inside your medicine packet.
Important

Do not take medicines called monoamine oxidase inhibitors or MAOIs with tramadol. Examples of MAOIs include moclobemide or phenelzine which are used to treat depression, or rasagiline or selegiline which are used to treat Parkinson's disease. The combination can cause serious side effects such as anxiety, confusion and hallucinations.
Taking tramadol with other painkillers
It's safe to take tramadol with paracetamol, ibuprofen or aspirin (aspirin is only suitable for people aged 16 and over).

Do not take medicines that contain codeine with tramadol because you are more likely to get side effects. This includes some painkillers you can buy from pharmacies, such as co-codamol, ibuprofen and codeine (Nurofen Plus) and Solpadeine.

There's very little information about taking complementary medicines, herbal remedies or supplements with tramadol. They're not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines. They're generally not tested for the effect they have on other medicines.
Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you're taking any other medicines, including herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.
